source: Orvalho & Kwiatkowska (2026, v3) Are LLMs Robust in Understanding Code Against Semantics-Preserving Mutations?
finding: Expert-labelled reasoning traces on LiveCodeBench output prediction. Code-tuned open models reach many correct answers through flawed reasoning; the two frontier closed models almost never do.
numbers: 9 LLMs, CoT traces labelled 3 times by experts blind to model. Correct predictions that were guesses/flawed: Llama3.2 55.1%, Mistral 50.0%, CodeGemma 44.7%, GraniteCode 43.1%, Qwen2.5-Coder 10.3%; GPT-5.2 0.2% and Gemini-3 0.2%. Accuracy: GPT-5.2 97.5%, Gemini-3 100%, Qwen2.5-Coder 62.6%.
quote: flawed reasoning in between 10% and 50% of cases
limits: Frontier near-ceiling scores may be benchmark contamination (LiveCodeBench 2024, models late 2025); authors say so. Python output prediction only. Expert analysis done on LiveCodeBench not CRUXEval.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the 'up to 60% flawed-but-correct' figure applies to small code models, not frontier. For a frontier agent, correct output prediction is mostly sound reasoning; do not budget a big cost for catching lucky guesses.

finding: Even the near-perfect frontier models collapse under structural but meaning-preserving rewrites, especially loop unrolling, loop-to-while and if-else swap.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, baseline to mutated: GPT-5.2 loop unrolling -68.1 points, Gemini-3 -70.4 (100% to 29.6%); Gemini-3 loop conversion -44.7, if-else swap -28.6, variable renaming -31.9 (100 to 68.1). CRUXEval: GPT-5.2 -43.8 (loop conversion), -63.0 (unrolling); Gemini-3 -47.6 / -52.4 (as printed in text). Drops up to 70% overall.
limits: Unrolled programs get longer, so part of the drop may be length, not semantics. Possible contamination makes the baseline unreliable (the model may recall the original).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: consistency across rewrites is a strong signal of fragility, but rewrites that change length can lower accuracy by themselves. Use cheap, length-neutral rewrites (rename, mirror comparison) for a consistency check.

source: Orvalho & Kwiatkowska (2026) prediction stability and renaming
finding: Some programs a model fails on become correct after a rewrite. This gives a pass-at-union gain for weaker models, almost none for frontier ones. Renaming gives the largest recovery.
numbers: LiveCodeBench extra programs solved by some mutation: SemCoder +36.5 (48.0 to over 84), Qwen2.5-Coder +29.4, Llama3.2 +26.9, Qwen3-Coder +14.8, GPT-5.2 +2.7, Gemini-3 0.0. CRUXEval: Llama3.2 +21.4, SemCoder +14.9, Gemini-3 +15.5, GPT-5.2 +4.6. Renaming alone: Qwen2.5-Coder 62.6 to 76.6 (+14.0), SemCoder +14.4, GPT-5.2 +1.5, but Gemini-3 100 to 68.1.
limits: They report union coverage, not a voting verifier. No test of majority vote across rewrites as an error detector.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 9: names matter in both directions (renaming helped weak models, hurt Gemini-3). A name-blind restatement is not shown safe. Consistency voting across rewrites is untested as a verifier; only the union upper bound exists.

finding: Same injected error is fixed far more often when attributed to the user than to the model itself. The blind spot is an activation gap, not missing knowledge.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average 64.5% blind spot. Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math domains (BIG-Bench Mistake): 62.8%. On models' own naturally generated errors, 4.3-10.8% of errors are caught if shown as external.
quote: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones
limits: Math/logic tasks, not code. Injected errors, not natural ones; the paper says the size is a property of the design. Single author. Most closed models cannot prefill, so few frontier models were tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: indirect evidence for own-output blindness. Treat self-verification of own code as weak; present the model's own code to the verifier as someone else's.

finding: Appending the word 'Wait' after the model's erroneous output restores most correction, matching reasoning-model versions. Fine-tuning on few error-correction traces also helps.
numbers: 'Wait' cuts blind spot by 89.3% and raises mean accuracy by 156%. 5,306 correction traces cut blind spot 76.0%. Macro accuracy base vs +Wait vs reasoning model: DeepSeek-V3 0.567/0.902/R1 0.908; Qwen3-32B 0.045/0.793/0.894; Qwen3-14B 0.117/0.868/0.843. Correction markers appear 179.5% more often after external errors (GSM8K-SC).
limits: Math. Reasoning models already show the effect mostly gone, so for current reasoning models the gain from 'Wait' is mostly absorbed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (by analogy): built-in reasoning absorbs a cheap prompt trick. A cheap re-evaluation trigger is a valid operator for non-reasoning models only.

source: Rajput, Chauhan, Kosaraju (2026) Cheap Verifiers, Large Blind Spots
finding: A verifier model waves through a large share of a student model's wrong answers. The share grows as the student gets stronger and shrinks as the verifier gets stronger.
numbers: Blind-spot rate rises 0.12 to 0.55 as student scales 0.5B to 32B (GSM8K, gpt-4o-mini verifier). Frontier verifier drops it to about 0.05 but escalates on 46% of hard MATH queries vs 39% true error rate. Dashboard through verifier reads about 3% error while true error swings up to 32%.
limits: Math answers, not code. Preprint, industry lab. Verifier is a different model, not self-verification.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a verifier of similar strength accepts many wrong answers. Do not read agent reliability from metrics computed by the agent's own verifier; use an independent oracle (tests, execution).

source: Olausson et al. (2024, ICLR) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are small once the cost of repair is counted. The bottleneck is the quality of the model's feedback on its own code.
numbers: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. Normalised pass rate vs i.i.d. sampling at equal budget is near 1 (heatmap cells such as 0.92-1.06). With a stronger model giving the feedback, gains are substantially larger. Human feedback vs GPT-4 feedback to GPT-3.5 repair success: overall 52.60% vs 33.30%; introductory 62.21 vs 42.64; interview 45.67 vs 19.33; competition 14.67 vs 3.67.
limits: 2023 models. Small human study. Newer reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and 6: model feedback on its own code is the weak link, in code. Equal-token comparison against resampling is the right test and self-repair mostly fails it. Execution output or an independent model should supply feedback.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and fix its answer does not help and sometimes hurts.
numbers: Abstract only read: performance 'at times even degrades after self-correction'. No figures taken.
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not recorded. Reasoning tasks (math, QA), pre-reasoning-model era; code was not the focus.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: supports the rule that verification needs an external signal. Same direction as d04 and d07.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD: Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging
finding: A hypothesise-predict-experiment-conclude loop with a real debugger (a hypothesis-first, scientific method scaffold) gives repair accuracy about the same as asking the LLM to patch directly, but adds explanations.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2: LLM-Base 87 plausible vs AutoSD 76; v2.0: 110 vs 113. Debugger ablation (LLM predicts execution output): share of runs with plausible patch 73% with real execution vs 63% when predicted. Human study 20 participants (6 professionals): explanation did not change time, accuracy improved on 5 of 6 bugs; 70% wanted explanations, 55% satisfied with scientific-debugging detail.
limits: Models of 2023 (davinci-002, ChatGPT). Human study small and mixed (14 students). Equal-token cost not reported; AutoSD uses more calls.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the closest direct test. Hypothesis-first prompting did not beat direct repair on accuracy; real execution results were what mattered (+10 points per run). Value is auditability and episode labels, not accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2024, ICLR) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Having the model explain its code line by line (rubber duck) and compare to the spec helps, with or without tests. Gains are largest when real execution feedback exists.
numbers: Spider (no unit tests): code explanation feedback +2-3% over baseline, +9% on hardest level. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Code explanation alone without debugging also consistently improves. Matches or beats baselines sampling more than 10x candidates.
limits: Codex/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era, few-shot prompts. Gains on Spider are small. No equal-token resampling ablation on all tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: an 'explain before judging' step has a small measured benefit for LLMs. This is the nearest LLM analogue of write-then-view; the human 4.7x effect is not tested.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed pipeline (file, then class/function, then edit lines, then repair) matches or beats open agents with coarse-to-fine localisation.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 32.00% (96 fixes) at $0.70. File-level localisation: prompting-based 78.7%, embedding-based 67.7%, combined 81.7%. Skipping the hierarchy (file straight to edit lines) is worse in cost and accuracy; full file content hurts localisation. Repair: greedy location set gives over 88 fixes; separate sampled location sets give 96.
limits: GPT-4o era, SWE-bench Lite only (300 Python issues); later agents with strong models exceed it. No larger repo tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: coarse-to-fine navigation helps at 2024 model level and SWE-bench scale; scaling to bigger repos and stronger models is untested here.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: Giving an agent a graph of files, classes, functions and call edges lets a fine-tuned 32B model match proprietary models on localisation at lower cost.
numbers: Up to 92.7% file-level accuracy; about 86% cost reduction; downstream issue resolution +12% at Pass@10.
limits: Abstract page only; benchmark details and baselines not extracted. Fine-tuned model, not a reading-strategy prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: structure-first navigation still pays in 2025, but through a graph tool, not a reading order. Supports 'fewer structural tools' only for a fine-tuned 32B model.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces
finding: Interface design (file viewer, search commands, guarded edit) changes agent success on SWE-bench.
numbers: Pass@1 12.5% on SWE-bench and 87.7% on HumanEvalFix. Per-component numbers not extracted (abstract only).
limits: Abstract page only. GPT-4 Turbo era.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: tool shape matters; this record has no test that fewer tools generalise beyond 7B.

source: Ma et al. (2024) An Empirical Study on LLM-based Agents for Automated Bug Fixing
finding: Across six SWE-bench Verified systems, file-level localisation accuracy tracks final resolve rate in rank order.
numbers: W&B Programmer localised at least one buggy file in 448 cases and all buggy files in 394; weakest (Learn-by-interact) 342, a 31.0% gap. Symbol level: 396 vs 308 (+28.6%). Ranking by file-level F1 matches ranking by resolve rate except Learn-by-interact.
limits: Localisation inferred from the final patch, not from agent reading steps. Six systems only. No test of any reading strategy.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: localisation is the step that predicts success, so labelled 'read/locate' episodes are the ones worth scoring. Trace labels were not validated here.

source: Liu et al. (2024) REval: Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM
finding: Models can give a correct output while contradicting themselves about the execution path. Consistency across related questions is low.
numbers: Average accuracy 44.4% on runtime behaviour reasoning; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3.
limits: Abstract only; 2024 code LLMs, not frontier.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: consistency across related questions about one program is a cheap check and was low for older models. Not tested on frontier reasoning models.

source: Majumdar et al. (2024) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for Code Reasoning
finding: Code reasoning ability (execution simulation, spec reasoning, semantics) does not correlate with bug-repair success; only advanced frontier models appear to use code reasoning when repairing.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 4 benchmarks. Bug repair performance not correlated with any of the code reasoning tasks.
limits: Abstract only read; correlation values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: comprehension scores and repair scores can be decoupled; a 'simulate' episode label is not enough evidence of success.

source: Soloway & Ehrlich (1984) Empirical Studies of Programming Knowledge, IEEE TSE 10(5)
finding: Not opened. Only existence and title confirmed through Crossref; the IEEE page returned empty. Exact percent-correct and N remain unverified.
limits: Gap 7 stays open. Do not cite any figure for this paper from this record.
agent_relevance: Keep plan-knowledge claims at single-source until the paper is read.

source: Pennington (1987) Stimulus structures and mental representations in expert comprehension of computer programs, Cognitive Psychology 19
finding: Not opened. DOI lookups failed (404); no abstract retrievable. Exact numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Keep program-model versus situation-model claims dependent on secondary reviews.

finding: No direct LLM test found for: hypothesis-first vs bottom-up reading at equal tokens (gap 1); logging Letovsky episode labels from agent traces (gap 4); write-then-view prediction (gap 6); ICSE 2025 student-attention papers (gap 10). WebSearch budget was exhausted; the arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited and arXiv search pages returned nothing.
numbers: Zero direct hits after about 10 targeted attempts.
limits: This is an absence of evidence from a restricted search, not proof that no such study exists.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 4, 6 and 10 as open and as candidate experiments for our own bench.
